title: Behavioral > Self-Reported Evidence
intro: Users are consistently unreliable narrators of their own behavior. Not because they're dishonest — because memory is reconstructive, social desirability is real, and people genuinely can't articulate why they do what they do.

learn.title: Two types of data, two different questions
learn.text:
**Self-reported data** (surveys, interviews, preference ratings) answers:
→ What do users **think**?

**Behavioral data** (task completion, clicks, time, errors) answers:
→ What do users **do**?

Conflating them leads to overconfident product decisions. They answer fundamentally different questions.

try.q: "82% of users said they were satisfied with the checkout flow." What type of evidence is this?
try.explain: Satisfaction ratings are self-reported data — they tell you what users THINK, not what they DO.

learn.title: Where the gap hits hardest
learn.text:
**Feature preferences:** Users say they want more features. Behavioral data shows they use fewer than they think.

**Task difficulty:** Users rate tasks as "easy" that actually took twice as long and produced twice the errors.

**Navigation confidence:** Users say they found what they looked for. Eye-tracking shows they scanned past it multiple times.

**Onboarding feedback:** Users say onboarding was clear. Activation and time-to-value data tells the real story.

try.q: Users rate a new feature as "easy to use" in a post-task survey, but task completion was only 40%. Which data point should drive your next design decision?
options: Discard both and survey more users
try.explain: Behavioral data (task completion) wins. Users genuinely can't accurately assess their own performance.

learn.title: Why this happens
learn.text:
It's not that users are liars. Three real mechanisms are at work:

**Reconstructive memory** — People don't replay events; they reconstruct them, filling gaps with what "must have" happened.

**Social desirability** — People answer the way they think a competent, attentive person would answer.

**Introspection limits** — People genuinely don't know or can't articulate why they do what they do. "I always read error messages" → they don't.

try.q: A user in a study says: "I carefully read all the error messages." Video shows they dismissed every error without reading. Why?
options: Social desirability — they're describing the ideal version of their behavior
They're deliberately lying to the researcher
try.explain: Social desirability: users describe how a competent person would behave, not what they actually did.

test.q: What does self-reported data primarily tell you?
options: What users think, feel, or believe
test.explain: Self-reported data captures attitudes, motivations, and preferences — not actual behavior.

test.q: Users say they prefer fewer features, but analytics show they use 12 features regularly. What's this an example of?
test.explain: Classic say–do gap: what users report about their behavior doesn't match their actual behavior.

test.q: Which of these is behavioral evidence?
test.explain: Task completion rate is behavioral — it measures what users did, not what they said.

test.q: Why are users "unreliable narrators" of their own behavior?
options: Reconstructive memory, social desirability, and introspection limits
They're not paying attention during studies
They want to sabotage the research
test.explain: Three mechanisms: memory reconstruction, desire to appear competent, and genuine inability to explain their own actions.

test.q: Post-study survey says onboarding was "clear and helpful." Activation data shows 60% of users never complete setup. What should you trust?
options: Activation data — behavioral evidence trumps self-report
The survey — users know their own experience
Neither — the sample size is too small
The survey — it's more recent data
test.explain: Behavioral data (activation rate) wins when it conflicts with self-report. Always.
